summary:
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts handling domestic affairs. Danish legislation on marriage and on official documents has been adopted and applies here, and the sources show a Greenland-specific procedure for changing the sex designation on identity papers.

Same-sex relations attract no criminal penalty in the sources, and the recorded social climate is quiet and non-violent. Reporting from May 2015 describes gay life as low-key, integrated and free of hostility, with a modest Pride march held in Nuuk since 2010. The first Pride parade took place in Nuuk on 15 May 2010 and drew about 1,000 people. The population is small and scattered, so there is virtually no organised gay scene; a handful of nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd.

Registered partnerships were available from 1 July 1996, when partnership legislation was adopted from the Danish model and passed with virtually no debate. That regime applied until the day the same-sex marriage law took effect on 1 April 2016, when the partnership law's application was repealed.

Same-sex marriage came into effect on 1 April 2016. The territory adopted Danish legislation that had passed unanimously on two occasions in Denmark, the first bill lapsing after Danish elections, and the local parliament enacted it without recorded opposition, replacing the 1996 partnership law. The bishop of the established church supported the change.

Transgender residents can change the sex designation on official identity documents under a law passed in 2016 by decree. Legal sex change rests on self-determination: no sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilisation or medical diagnosis is required. Applicants must be over 18 and state that they want their documentation changed, then observe a six-month reflection period to confirm the request.

Greenlandic passports are available with an "X" sex descriptor alongside male and female.

Hate speech has been outlawed since 2010. Article 100 of the Criminal Code prohibits speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories, and the code provides penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. Whether these provisions name gender identity explicitly is not stated in the sources.

Parliament passed a Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination in May 2024, in force from 1 July 2024, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics among other characteristics. The law creates an Equal Treatment Board to manage discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination.

The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland works closely with the Danish Institute for Human Rights to promote and protect human rights.
tangentialFactors:
The territory's reform pattern follows Denmark closely. The 1996 partnership law and the 2016 marriage law were both adopted from Danish legislation, and the marriage bill passed the local parliament without recorded opposition after clearing the Danish parliament unanimously twice.

Public visibility has grown steadily rather than through confrontation. A Pride march has run in Nuuk since 2010, the inaugural parade drew about 1,000 attendees, and organised advocacy now has a national body with a trans-inclusive remit. Reporting frames gay life as socially unremarkable rather than celebratory.

The small and dispersed population shapes the local scene more than legal restriction does. There is virtually no gay scene outside Nuuk, and social life runs through mixed venues rather than segregated ones.
localsOnly:
LGBT Qaamaneq, a national association for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, was founded in August 2014. It works for political, cultural and social equality and is open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters, so allies can join alongside members.

The former partnership status was known as nalunaarsukkamik inooqatigiinneq and ran from 1 July 1996 until 1 April 2016, when the marriage law took over and the partnership law's application was repealed.

Legal gender change is an administrative process rather than a medical one. An applicant over 18 states the request, waits six months to confirm it, and then receives updated documentation; no diagnosis, surgery, hormones or sterilisation are involved.

Discrimination complaints on grounds including gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics may be taken to the Equal Treatment Board established by the Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination, in force 1 July 2024. The same law sets up an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination.

Residents seeking human rights support can reach the Human Rights Council of Greenland, which is state-funded and works with the Danish Institute for Human Rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Greenland's own Criminal Code and Danish criminal statutes operate in parallel, and exactly which Danish statutes extend to Greenland beyond those adopted by reference, is not resolved by these sources. The inventory does not address the decriminalisation of same-sex relations directly.

Article 100 is described as covering sexual orientation among other categories; the full list of protected grounds, including whether gender identity is named, is not sourced here. No enforcement record for Article 100, for the hate-crime penalty enhancements or for the Equal Treatment Board is available, so complaint handling and outcomes remain unverified.

The 2016 decree on legal sex change is summarised from secondary coverage; the instrument's full text, its interaction with Danish national rules, and any subsequent amendment are unresolved.

No source in this inventory covers entry or visa screening, airport or border document checks, restroom and facility rules, or access to hormones, surgical care and other trans-specific health services for visitors. Nothing is stated about partner or spousal recognition in immigration or residency matters.
